paper.title: Grounding User Preferences in Shared Multimodal Concepts for Recommendation
paper.summary: Multimodal recommendation has substantially advanced item understanding by incorporating rich visual and textual content. Yet user preferences are still commonly encoded as implicit signals tied to individual items, leaving recurring semantic factors without persistent identities that can be shared across items. We introduce MKGE, a multimodal knowledge graph framework that represents these factors as canonical, addressable concepts. MKGE induces a domain-adaptive concept vocabulary from item images and titles, grounds each user's interaction history in supported concepts, and jointly models direct user-item evidence and concept-mediated preference signals. By turning recurring semantics into shared coordinates, MKGE enables evidence from different items to accumulate around the same preference factors. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that MKGE consistently outperforms collaborative, knowledge-graph, multimodal, and recent LLM/MLLM-based recommenders across all six reported metrics. Controlled studies further demonstrate the importance of canonical concept identities and personalized user-concept correspondence, with especially pronounced gains over removing or rewiring the user graph for low-activity users. These results establish canonical multimodal concepts as effective units for preference modeling and transfer. Code, constructed knowledge graphs, and prompts are available at https://github.com/Garden1a-X/MKGE.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitation of implicit, item-bound preference encoding in multimodal recommendation by introducing canonical, addressable concepts. By grounding user interactions in a shared multimodal knowledge graph, it enables preference signals to accumulate across items, significantly improving recommendation accuracy, especially for low-activity users.

paper.title: OneQuery: Unified Sequence-to-Structure Generation for Multilingual E-commerce Query Understanding
paper.summary: Multilingual e-commerce search requires robust query understanding to convert cross-lingual user queries with varied linguistic patterns into standardized semantic representations that support retrieval and ranking. However, traditional Query Understanding systems suffer from error accumulation, separately optimized subtasks that ignore their mutual correlations, and high maintenance costs. To address these issues, this paper proposes OneQuery, a unified generative framework for multilingual query understanding based on domain-specific large language models in e-commerce. We reformulate four subtasks, namely Language Recognition, Spelling Correction, Translation, and Query Tagging, into a unified Sequenceto-Structure autoregressive generation process constrained by predefined schemas, and design a three-stage progressive training pipeline with multi-task reinforcement learning alignment. OneQuery demonstrates consistent gains over baselines across all tasks and remains effective across different backbone sizes, and online experiments in the AliExpress e-commerce search scenario further confirm its practical value for industrial deployment.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Modularity and error propagation in multi-stage NLP pipelines for cross-lingual semantic normalization.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper proposes a unified generative framework that consolidates multiple query understanding subtasks into a single autoregressive process, reducing system complexity and maintenance overhead. By leveraging domain-specific LLMs and reinforcement learning, it improves the robustness of cross-lingual search in industrial e-commerce settings.

key_metrics.baseline: Traditional separately optimized subtask baselines

paper.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
paper.summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

analysis.problem_statement: The scarcity of accepted reasoning traces for hard mathematical problems under independent Monte Carlo sampling limits the effectiveness of post-training large language models.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data efficiency and coverage in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or supervised fine-tuning for complex reasoning tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the 'hard problem' bottleneck in LLM math reasoning where standard sampling fails to generate correct solutions, limiting training data diversity. By mining rejected traces to generate diverse alternatives, DART significantly increases the number of solvable problems without increasing computational cost. This enables more effective post-training of smaller models, improving performance on benchmarks like AIME and MATH-500.

key_metrics.baseline: Independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling at matched number of generated traces

technical_breakdown.method: DART starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into steps, ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty, and generates distinct alternative candidates for high-uncertainty steps using reference-answer guidance and meta-thoughts to complete the trace.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical to baseline; cost per accepted trace is 30% lower.

paper.title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
paper.summary: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.

paper.title: Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. These findings show that high accuracy on pre-aligned, ordered inputs does not establish that a model uses timestamps to synchronize observations with the world. We release our code, model outputs, and trajectory labels at https://github.com/tingrui-huang/timestamps-matter.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper exposes a critical flaw in current time series reasoning evaluations by demonstrating that high model accuracy often persists even when timestamps are removed or replaced, indicating reliance on shortcuts rather than true temporal grounding. It introduces a diagnostic protocol to differentiate timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational biases, revealing that models rarely detect incorrect timestamps when context is pre-aligned.

paper.title: Routeability Before Routing: Routeability Audit Protocol (RAP) and RouteabilityBench for Audited LLM Model Selection
paper.summary: LLM routing aims to choose, for each prompt, which model in a portfolio is most likely to answer correctly. This only makes sense when the benchmark contains enough prompt-specific variation for different models to be best on different inputs. On coarse-scored LLM benchmarks, however, many models often tie for the best score, and the single best model may already leave little room for improvement. We therefore propose a routeability-first audit, instantiated as RAP and RouteabilityBench, a runnable claim-verification package. The audit is retrospective: it runs once the benchmark-portfolio score matrix exists and before router comparisons are interpreted as general evidence, rather than certifying a portfolio that has not yet been evaluated. Across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, generic routing enhancements such as larger embedding sets, dimensionality reduction, selective abstention, clustering, and stronger regressors do not consistently outperform the single best model. The clearest positive evidence is concentrated in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval show different ways in which routing can remain hard or predictor-sensitive. Our practical recommendation is that routing gains should be reported together with routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio construction details, and family-corrected statistical tests.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation validity and statistical rigor in model selection and routing strategies.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces a 'routeability-first' audit protocol to verify whether a benchmark portfolio actually supports routing gains before interpreting router comparisons. It demonstrates that generic routing enhancements frequently fail to outperform the single best model on coarse-scored benchmarks, highlighting the need for rigorous diagnostics in LLM evaluation.

key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not quantifiable as a single percentage; findings indicate routing does not consistently outperform the baseline.

paper.title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior
paper.summary: Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.

analysis.problem_statement: How to transfer the beneficial optimization geometry (initialization 'fate') from one neural network architecture to another without transferring learned features, gradients, or labels.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Optimization landscape sensitivity to architecture and initialization, specifically the inability of shallow or coarse-grained networks to naturally acquire the representational benefits of deeper or finer-grained architectures during training.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a method to decouple a model's optimization trajectory from its physical structure by aligning its initial representational geometry to a randomly initialized guide network. This allows shallow networks to inherit the optimization benefits of depth and coarse networks to gain finer representational granularity, improving downstream performance without additional training data or gradient flow from the guide.

key_metrics.baseline: Standard random initialization of the target network.
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not specified in the provided abstract.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The alignment procedure references the guide network's geometry to shape the target network's initialization. It is label-free and gradient-free with respect to the guide network, ensuring no feature transfer occurs, only geometric alignment.

paper.title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
paper.summary: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and safety in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection for foundation models, specifically addressing the 'silent failure' bottleneck in deployment monitoring.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in monitoring tabular foundation models, which often fail silently when encountering distribution shifts. By introducing CALD, a lightweight unsupervised monitor, it enables real-time detection of harmful shifts without requiring test labels. This is significant for the current AI landscape as it enhances the trustworthiness of tabular models in high-stakes deployment scenarios where data drift is common.

paper.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
paper.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Security and robustness in multimodal AI decision-making processes, specifically regarding inference-time manipulation of content-aware recommenders.
analysis.executive_summary: This work challenges the prevailing assumption that multimodal compression and fusion enhance robustness against manipulation, revealing instead that they can amplify specific signals to create exploitable biases. By introducing C3H, an inference-time attack that aligns target item content with implicit decision criteria, the paper demonstrates a significant security risk in current MLLM-based recommender architectures.

key_metrics.baseline: Standard multimodal LLM recommender systems without C3H attack

paper.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
paper.summary: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.

paper.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
paper.summary: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

paper.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
paper.summary: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of cross-platform generalization and long-horizon task execution in autonomous agents.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark that tests agents on realistic, multi-step workflows spanning Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web. It reveals that current frontier models, while strong on Linux, significantly underperform humans on mobile and macOS platforms, highlighting a critical gap in platform-robust autonomy.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Versioned task releases (v1), trajectory logging, and final-state evaluation logic that verifies durable changes rather than just action sequences.

paper.title: Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting
paper.summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The lack of effective mechanisms for incorporating external multimodal context (text) into frozen, pre-trained time-series foundation models, which typically rely on input concatenation or intermediate representation fusion.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a parameter-efficient adaptation method that allows frozen time-series foundation models to leverage textual context by generating temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates. By keeping both the numerical backbone and text encoder frozen, it offers a robust, zero-shot capable approach to multimodal forecasting that exactly recovers original model behavior when context is absent.

key_metrics.baseline: Frozen TSFM and Static LoRA baselines

paper.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
paper.summary: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

paper.title: Benefit of Structured Representations: When Equivariance Helps in Image Classification
paper.summary: Equivariant neural networks promise improved representation learning through structural guarantees. However, mainstream vision encoders rarely incorporate equivariance for most geometric symmetries. Images are a particularly interesting modality with many such symmetries and extensive datasets from which to learn this structure. In this work, we investigate when vision encoders benefit from geometric inductive biases. We study the discrete rotation group of quarter-turns (C4) which acts losslessly without interpolation or boundary artifacts. Combined with image classification as a controlled invariant objective, this allows for a principled empirical investigation into the role of structural guarantees. We introduce ConvNeXt-C4 as a rotation equivariant ConvNeXt with dimension-equivalent yet orientation-structured representations. Training from scratch, our experiments show, that the C4 variant outperforms its base model across all tasks while operating with 6x fewer parameters and 1.6x fewer FLOPs. Its performance advantage increases log-linearly with decreasing training set size, with pre-training providing a similar improvement across both model variants. Analyzing the classifier head reveals that orientation information from the representations' structure is actively used, improving performance by 4.90% across all datasets. Our results highlight the sample-efficiency benefits of equivariance and the value of retained orientation information, motivating further investigation beyond image classification. Code is available at https://github.com/hlzl/equivariant-convnext.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Sample efficiency and data scarcity in representation learning for computer vision tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that structured, equivariant representations can significantly outperform standard encoders while using substantially fewer parameters and computational resources. By leveraging the discrete rotation group C4, the model achieves better generalization, particularly in low-data regimes, highlighting the value of explicit geometric inductive biases in modern vision architectures.

paper.title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
paper.summary: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

paper.title: Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification
paper.summary: Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that places role-separated LLM agents inside a formal-methods-inspired claim-obligation-certificate protocol. Given a generation candidate, Agent-as-a-Verifier produces a certificate by extracting a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiling the task's acceptance contract, and deriving checkable obligations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Agent-as-a-Verifier achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art approach. Across different downstream applications, the augmented agent also outperforms the plain agent on FrontierMath and CyberGym. More importantly, Agent-as-a-Verifier is able to identify reward-hacking solutions that deceive the benchmark evaluator, highlighting its broader potential for iterative and recursive agent optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/sunyxedu/General-Verifier

paper.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
paper.summary: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The sparsity and discreteness of feed-forward pointmap methods, which limit geometric accuracy and detail preservation in pose-free 3D reconstruction.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in computer vision by enabling generalizable, zero-shot 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images. By integrating pointmap priors with ray-based representations, it overcomes the limitations of sparse point clouds, offering a foundation model approach that significantly improves geometric fidelity and detail preservation compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paper.title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
paper.summary: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation reliability and simulator fidelity in complex, stateful conversational tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in evaluating conversational AI where simulators fail to maintain consistency in multi-step workflows, causing false negatives in assistant performance. By introducing a benchmark based on Hierarchical Task Networks and a state-tracking prompting strategy, it provides a more robust framework for assessing assistant capabilities in realistic, complex scenarios.

key_metrics.baseline: Standard LLM-based user simulators without state tracking

paper.title: On the Learnability of Model Reprogramming: A Reachability and Relabeling Perspective
paper.summary: Model reprogramming adapts a frozen source model to a target task by wrapping it in a learnable input transformation from target input to the source-model input space, and an output mapping from source-model outputs to target predictions. Despite extensive empirical progress, the finite-sample learnability of the induced wrapper hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ remains underexplored. We address this for source models that expose hard source labels and analyze it through the wrapper structure: on any target samples, the input transformation selects reachable source labels that the output mapping relabels. Through this lens, we answer two questions: (1) how many target samples are needed to approach the best predictor in $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$, and (2) what gap remains between the optimum over $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ and the target Bayes risk. For (1), the wrapper structure factorizes the sample-wise complexity of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ into a reachability term counting reachable source-label patterns, and a conditional relabeling term counting their relabelings. This yields an agnostic-PAC bound on the estimation error, with sample complexity scaling additively in the two terms; this bound becomes closed-form on additive input transformations and is matched by a lower bound on an explicit binary classification construction. For (2), the same structure decomposes the approximation error exactly into the source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction with a source-conditional upper bound on this gap. We extend the approximation analysis to logit-exposing source models, where the upper bound is empirically estimable. The wrapper-side analysis localizes both errors to specific components, giving a structural view of reprogramming practice.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of theoretical understanding regarding the finite-sample learnability and approximation error of model reprogramming, specifically for source models that expose hard labels.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Theoretical gap in understanding the statistical efficiency and generalization bounds of wrapper-based model adaptation methods.
analysis.executive_summary: This work provides the first rigorous PAC-Bayes style analysis of model reprogramming, decomposing the learning problem into reachability and relabeling components. It establishes that sample complexity scales additively with the number of reachable source-label patterns and their relabelings, offering a structural explanation for why certain reprogramming strategies succeed or fail.

key_metrics.baseline: Standard PAC learning bounds for general hypothesis classes

They derive an agnostic-PAC bound for estimation error and an exact decomposition for approximation error into source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Analysis of additive input transformations yields closed-form bounds. The approximation analysis is extended to logit-exposing source models, where the upper bound on the gap to Bayes risk is empirically estimable.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Theoretical analysis; no specific computational complexity for training is provided, but sample complexity is shown to scale additively with reachability and relabeling terms.

paper.title: Hybrid Reinforcement Learning for One-step Degraded Infrared and Visible Image Fusion
paper.summary: Infrared and visible image fusion (IVIF) is essential for robust perception, yet existing methods remain limited under complex degradations. While diffusion models (DMs) offer powerful modeling capabilities to combat such degradations, their iterative process incurs high computational cost. One-step distillation effectively accelerates inference but typically leads to over-smoothed results. To resolve these limitations, we propose a one-step fusion framework with hybrid reinforcement learning, termed OneHRL. We treat degraded inputs as intermediate noisy states along a generative trajectory, enabling a distilled one-step generator to rectify them directly to the clean fusion results. Concurrently, to mitigate the over-smoothed results in distillation, we incorporate the Flow-GRPO paradigm to introduce stochasticity into the deterministic one-step generation. This restores the stochastic exploration necessary for sampling-based reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we design a coarse-to-fine reward that integrates a global semantic reward with an object-level reward. This hybrid reward ensures that the generator captures both naturalness and fine-grained texture. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior fusion quality and efficiency.

paper.title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
paper.summary: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: High computational cost and failure rates of global retraining for safety verification and adaptation in dynamic environments.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in deploying safe neural network controllers in dynamic environments where static safety guarantees become invalid due to new obstacles. By framing adaptation as a localized repair problem, it enables real-time safety updates that are significantly faster and more reliable than traditional retraining methods, enhancing the practicality of formally safe AI systems.

paper.title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
paper.summary: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.

analysis.problem_statement: Conventional post-processing of parallel annealing results typically refines only the single best candidate, failing to exploit the diversity of the generated population to discover superior solutions.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient utilization of solution diversity in stochastic optimization post-processing, leading to suboptimal convergence in combinatorial problems.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the underutilization of candidate diversity in parallel annealing by introducing a deterministic, training-free refinement method. It demonstrates that exploiting the full population through iterative path-relinking can outperform additional annealing time, offering a reliable way to improve solution quality without modifying the underlying stochastic process.

key_metrics.baseline: Conventional single-candidate polishing and additional annealing time

technical_breakdown.architecture: A post-processing module that operates on the output population of a parallel annealer, utilizing path-relinking heuristics and iterative population updates.

paper.title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
paper.summary: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression. Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper seeks to theoretically explain the double-descent phenomenon in deep learning, specifically why test loss peaks near the interpolation threshold, by reframing it through the lens of universal compression and the gap between Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and Bayes-optimal prediction.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Theoretical understanding of generalization in over-parameterized deep learning models, particularly the failure of classical bias-variance tradeoff explanations to account for the double-descent peak.
analysis.executive_summary: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework linking the double-descent peak to the discrepancy between MLE and Bayes-optimal predictors, suggesting that the peak is driven by the cost of using MLE (e.g., via SGD) rather than ensemble methods. It offers a new perspective on why modern deep learning models can generalize well despite interpolating training data, moving beyond empirical observations to a compression-based explanation.

key_metrics.metric_value: SGD cross-entropy is roughly 4x SGLD ensemble cross-entropy; SGLD ensemble remains near log(10)

paper.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
paper.summary: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in the evaluation of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) by introducing CovNovBench, a benchmark specifically designed to test performance under covariate novelty. paper.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
paper.summary: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.

paper.title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
paper.summary: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 °C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.

paper.title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
paper.summary: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.

paper.title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
paper.summary: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.

paper.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
paper.summary: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $ε$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-γ)^{-1},(1-γ)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $γ$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-γ)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $δ\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Theoretical sample efficiency gaps and incomplete lower bound coverage in robust reinforcement learning.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper resolves a significant theoretical gap in robust reinforcement learning by providing tighter and complete sample complexity bounds for KL-divergence uncertainty sets. It improves upon existing upper bounds and extends lower bounds to all uncertainty levels, offering a more precise understanding of the data requirements for robust policy optimization.

paper.title: L2C2: Enhancing Large-scale Chiplets for Agent Long-Context LLM Inference with Sparse and Distributed Attention
paper.summary: Long-context inference is a rising demand for LLMs, especially for agent applications. Sparse attention (SpAt) and chiplet technology are promising solutions to reduce computations and scale hardware performance. However, deploying SpAt on distributed chiplets necessitates context parallelism for workload partitioning, introducing complex distributed attention. In this work, we present L2C2, a system optimization for distributed SpAt in long-context inference. During the partial-prefill stage, we propose a novel Split-Comm Attention mechanism that leverages the high-bandwidth interconnect of chiplets to trade communication overhead for reduced memory access. We combine it with conventional Ring Attention to form a Bi-Mode method that adapts to varying input sequence lengths. During the decoding stage, we analyze the cause of memory access imbalance and address it by static interleaved token assignment. Dynamic agile cache balancing is also proposed to adapt to SpAt skewness. Evaluations show our optimization can achieve 1.45$\times$ and 1.53$\times$ speedup in partial-prefill and decoding with SpAt on large-scale chiplets.

analysis.executive_summary: This work is significant for the scaling of LLMs to agent applications requiring long contexts by optimizing hardware-software co-design. It leverages chiplet interconnects to mitigate the memory bottlenecks inherent in distributed sparse attention, enabling more efficient inference on next-generation modular hardware.

paper.title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
paper.summary: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.

paper.title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?
paper.summary: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that while self-evolving frameworks like AgentEvolver and Autogenesis improve agent performance, they fail to close the performance gap between English and Urdu. It reveals that RL-based evolution can even degrade Urdu reasoning relative to English, highlighting that language parity is not an emergent property of self-improvement but requires explicit design intervention.

paper.title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance
paper.summary: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

paper.title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
paper.summary: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately identifying and linking standard and optional car features in advertisement text to a specific vehicle's feature catalogue, where sellers use varied and inconsistent terminology for the same feature.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data scarcity and annotation cost for domain-specific Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Entity Linking tasks, specifically in the automotive domain where feature naming is highly variable.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces a hybrid corpus combining human-verified gold data with LLM-generated silver data, demonstrating a robust pipeline for auto-annotation that mitigates LLM hallucinations through validation and model escalation. It provides a benchmark for contextual NER in a niche domain, showing that smaller, fine-tuned LLMs can outperform traditional encoder architectures, particularly on unseen features.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Span F1 score on advert-disjoint splits
key_metrics.baseline: Fine-tuned encoder model (59.0% Span F1)

technical_breakdown.method: The task is formulated as feature-conditioned (contextual) NER, where the model extracts spans corresponding to specific catalogue features. The corpus is built using a two-layer approach: a human-gold layer and an LLM-silver layer. The LLM annotation process includes a validation loop where malformed outputs are patched, hallucinations trigger retries with stronger models, and out-of-candidate links are dropped. The LLM is only used for solo annotation after its agreement with human annotators matches human-human agreement levels.
technical_breakdown.architecture: The evaluation compares a LoRA-tuned 4B parameter LLM against a fine-tuned encoder model. The LLM approach is the primary proposed method for high-performance extraction.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) for efficient fine-tuning of the LLM, a search-grounded LLM for auto-annotation, and a specific validation protocol that counts and drops links to features outside the candidate list. The dataset consists of 430 human-annotated and 925 LLM-annotated adverts.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The use of a 4B parameter LLM with LoRA suggests moderate computational requirements for fine-tuning, significantly lower than full fine-tuning of large models but higher than training small encoder models. The annotation pipeline involves iterative validation and potential model escalation, adding complexity to the data generation phase.

paper.title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models
paper.summary: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the gap in adapting efficient hybrid models to diffusion generation, which is crucial for balancing performance and computational efficiency in modern LLMs. By introducing DiCALM, it enables faster generation speeds while maintaining comparable performance to autoregressive baselines, offering a viable path for deploying efficient diffusion-based language models.

paper.title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
paper.summary: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We stress-test this assumption with NONSENSE, a black-box optimization framework that constructs visibly non-semantic strings by optimizing only their dense similarity to the query. Across seven retrieval datasets and five single-vector retrievers, these strings frequently outscore the retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP) and often rank first in the full corpus. The result indicates a semanticity gap in the evaluated dense retrievers: strings with no coherent passage-level semantic content can lie closer to the query in embedding space than genuine relevant evidence. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating dense retrievers not only by whether they retrieve relevant documents, but also by whether their similarity scores reliably reflect semantic evidence.

analysis.problem_statement: Dense retrieval models exhibit a 'semanticity gap' where high embedding similarity does not guarantee semantic relevance, allowing non-semantic strings to outscore genuine relevant passages.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability of similarity scoring in embedding spaces and robustness of dense retrievers against adversarial or degenerate inputs.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that current dense retrievers are vulnerable to non-semantic strings that exploit the geometry of embedding spaces to achieve high similarity scores without any actual semantic content. By showing that these 'nonsense' strings can rank above the best relevant passages, the work highlights a critical flaw in using raw similarity scores as a proxy for relevance in search and RAG systems.

key_metrics.baseline: Retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP)

technical_breakdown.architecture: Seven retrieval datasets and five single-vector retrievers used for evaluation; no specific model architecture is proposed, only an attack/evaluation framework.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Optimization of string embeddings to lie closer to the query in embedding space than genuine relevant evidence; black-box approach implies gradient-free or query-based optimization.

paper.title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
paper.summary: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing sparse autoencoder and cross-layer interpretation methods lack an explicit training objective that forces sparse features at one layer to predict the sparse features at the subsequent layer, limiting the ability to model sequential feature evolution.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Interpretability and controllability of internal representations in large language models.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces Sparse-to-Sparse (S2S) feature learning, a method that explicitly trains intermediate sparse features to predict those in the next layer, thereby enhancing the structural coherence of the model's internal representation. By anchoring the final layer to the output distribution and optimizing sequentially from output to input, S2S provides a more robust framework for feature-based interventions and steering compared to standard sparse-feature baselines.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Adjacent-layer correspondence and separation of steering-induced effects from reconstruction effects
key_metrics.baseline: Matched sparse-feature baselines

technical_breakdown.method: Sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict the sparse codes of the immediately following layer. The final layer is anchored by an output-distribution loss, and optimization proceeds sequentially from the output layer back to the input layer.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) applied across multiple layers with a cross-layer prediction objective (S2S).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Sequential optimization from output to input; evaluation via feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift; causal ablation for complementary evidence.

paper.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
paper.summary: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing deep learning models for beat and downbeat tracking are primarily designed for offline processing, making them unsuitable for real-time, low-latency applications.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Latency and causality constraints in real-time audio processing pipelines.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper bridges the gap between high-accuracy offline beat tracking and the strict causality requirements of live performance systems. By adapting the 'Beat This' model into a causal variant that predicts future beats, it significantly reduces effective latency while improving accuracy over current online state-of-the-art methods.

paper.title: Autonomous Vineyard Exploration using LiDAR Sensing: A Field Evaluation on Legged-Wheeled Quadruped Robot
paper.summary: Autonomous navigation in vineyards presents significant challenges due to uneven terrain, sparse vegetation, and the repetitive geometric nature of vineyard rows. This paper evaluates a LiDAR-based autonomous exploration system deployed on a Unitree Go2 Wheeled quadruped robot. Our approach utilizes an iterative RANSAC-based line detection pipeline to identify vineyard rows and a finite-state navigation strategy to govern row selection and traversal. Field evaluations conducted at Denbies Vineyard (UK) demonstrate the system's ability to perform sustained autonomous row following, completing a 370m up-and-down traversal without intervention. We analyze the failure modes encountered, specifically focusing on line detection instability in sparse vegetation and the trade-offs of spatial filtering. The results suggest that, while RANSAC provides a robust geometric primitive, additional temporal filtering and adaptive perception are required for reliable lane-to-lane transitions in commercial vineyard environments. A video of the experimental results is available at: youtu.be/1om1HFGF4ps

analysis.problem_statement: Achieving reliable autonomous navigation and row-following in vineyards with uneven terrain and sparse vegetation using LiDAR sensing on a legged-wheeled quadruped robot.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Perception robustness and navigation stability in unstructured, repetitive agricultural environments with sparse geometric features.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical challenge of deploying autonomous robots in complex agricultural settings by demonstrating a LiDAR-based system on a Unitree Go2 robot. It highlights the limitations of standard RANSAC line detection in sparse vegetation, providing valuable insights into the gap between theoretical geometric robustness and practical field reliability for agri-robotics.

key_metrics.baseline: Manual intervention or non-autonomous operation

technical_breakdown.method: The system employs an iterative RANSAC-based line detection pipeline to identify vineyard rows from LiDAR point clouds, coupled with a finite-state machine to manage row selection and traversal logic.
